newsitem.title: USA: US July PPI more evidence of stellar inflation.
newsitem.headline: US July PPI more evidence of stellar inflation.

text.p: U.S. producer prices remained surprisingly subdued at every stage of processing in July, providing further evidence that strong growth and low unemployment are not necessarily a formula for rising U.S. inflation.

The Labor Department reported on Wednesday that overall producer prices fell by 0.1 percent in July, a record seventh consecutive decline. Even more reassuring, however, was a 0.2 percent decline in prices at the intermediate goods level and a 0.1 percent decrease in crude goods prices -- the so-called "pipeline" prices which tend to signal future inflation.

"From top to bottom this is a great report," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. "In time we should get a moderate increase in price pressures, but particularly on the goods side of the economy the numbers are spectacular right now."
Wall Street economists polled by Reuters had been calling for a 0.1 percent increase in the headline and core reading -- which excludes the volatile food and energy readings.
And in the wake of a substantial increase in the price component of the National Association of Purchasing Management July report, many had expected a rise in core crude prices.
But these prices declined by 0.5 percent in July, more than offsetting a 0.4 percent increase last month.
A strong dollar and increased global competition were cited as reasons for the confoundingly stellar inflation news, which has persisted amid robust growth and historically low unemployment levels.
"The overall message is that inflation at just about every stage of processing is still under control," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank.
"We have to respect the fact that in this environment the strength of the dollar continues to be a factor which limits the ability of producers in globally traded goods to raise prices," he added.

In the July producer price report, virtually every sector declined at the finished goods level, with gasoline prices down 1.0 percent, heating oil prices shrinking 3.4 percent and automobiles down 1.6 percent.

Economists have virtually discounted the possibility of further monetary tightening at the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting on August 19, and Wednesday's price report reinforced expectations of steady policy.
On Thursday, the Labor Department will release its July consumer price report. Economists are calling for an increase of 0.2 percent in the headline and core readings.
